title: Hello, Name!
brief: Builds a friendly greeting using the given name.
description: Take the name that is passed in and glue it between the word 'Hello ' and an exclamation point. It works no matter what the name is, even an empty one.
solution:
def hello_name(name):
    return "Hello " + name + "!"
hints: You just need to stick three pieces together with +.
Remember the space after 'Hello' and the '!' at the very end.
explainer: Adding strings with + just lines them up in order, so "Hello " + name + "!" always produces the greeting shape.

title: Make ABBA
brief: Wraps one string around two copies of another string.
description: Given two strings a and b, build a new string in the pattern a, b, b, a. Think of it like a sandwich where b is the filling, doubled, and a is the bread on both sides.
solution:
def make_abba(a, b):
    return a + b + b + a
hints: There are four pieces to line up: a, b, b, a.
You can write b twice, or use b + b once.
explainer: Concatenating strings in the exact order a, b, b, a always produces the abba pattern, regardless of how long each piece is.

title: Make Tags
brief: Wraps a word in an opening and closing HTML-style tag.
description: Given a tag name and a word, build a string that looks like <tag>word</tag>. The closing tag uses the same tag name with a forward slash in front of it.
solution:
def make_tags(tag, word):
    return "<" + tag + ">" + word + "</" + tag + ">"
hints: You need six pieces total: <, tag, >, word, </, tag, > — count them carefully.
The closing piece reuses the tag string with a / added before it.
explainer: Since tag is just a string, we can reuse it twice: once for the opening bracket and once for the closing bracket with a slash.

title: Make Out Word
concept: Slicing to insert into the middle of a string
brief: Slips a word inside another string, right after its first two characters.
description: Given an outer string and a word, insert the word between the first two characters of the outer string and the rest of it. The outer string acts like a little pocket that opens after its second letter.
solution:
def make_out_word(out, word):
    return out[:2] + word + out[2:]
hints: Slice out into two parts: the first 2 characters and everything after.
The word you insert goes right between those two slices.
explainer: out[:2] grabs the first two characters and out[2:] grabs the remainder, so putting word between those two slices reassembles out with word tucked inside.

title: Extra End
brief: Grabs the last two characters of a string and repeats them three times.
description: Take the last two characters of the given string and print them back to back three times in a row. This still works even if the string is shorter than two characters.
solution:
def extra_end(s):
    return s[-2:] * 3
hints: Negative slicing like s[-2:] grabs characters counting from the end.
Multiplying a string by 3 repeats it three times in a row.
explainer: s[-2:] safely returns the last two characters, or the whole string if it's shorter, and multiplying by 3 stacks three copies together.

title: First Two
concept: Safe slicing shorter than requested length
brief: Returns the first two characters of a string, or the whole thing if it's shorter.
description: Return the first two letters of the given string. If the string only has zero or one letters, just return the whole string as it is.
solution:
def first_two(s):
    return s[:2]
hints: Python slicing never crashes even when you ask for more characters than exist.
s[:2] alone handles every case here, including empty strings.
explainer: Slicing with s[:2] simply stops early if the string is too short, so it naturally handles empty and one-character strings.

title: First Half
brief: Returns the first half of a string, rounding the midpoint down for odd lengths.
description: Return just the first half of the given string. If the string has an odd number of characters, drop the extra middle character rather than including it.
solution:
def first_half(s):
    return s[:len(s) // 2]
hints: Find the string's length first, then cut it in half using integer division //.
Integer division rounds down, which conveniently drops any leftover middle character.
explainer: len(s) // 2 rounds down to the nearest whole number, so slicing up to that point always leaves out any extra middle character on odd-length strings.

title: Without End
concept: Slicing off both ends of a string
brief: Removes the first and last character of a string.
description: Return the given string with its very first and very last characters removed. You can assume the string always has at least 2 characters to work with.
solution:
def without_end(s):
    return s[1:-1]
hints: Slicing can start after index 0 and stop before the last index at the same time.
s[1:-1] skips the first character and stops one before the last.
explainer: The slice s[1:-1] begins at index 1, skipping the first character, and ends right before the final index, skipping the last character too.

title: Combine Strings
brief: Joins two strings together, putting the shorter one first.
description: Given two strings, join them so that the shorter one comes first. If both strings are the same length, just join them in the order they were given, first string then second.
hints: Compare len(a) and len(b) to figure out which one is shorter.
Don't forget the tie case: equal lengths join in the original a-then-b order.
explainer: Comparing the lengths tells us which string is shorter, and we place that one first; when the lengths match we fall back to the plain a + b order.

title: Non Start
concept: Dropping the first character before joining
brief: Joins two strings together after removing the first letter from each.
description: Given two strings, chop off the first character of each one, then glue the two leftover pieces together. If a string is empty or just one character, its leftover piece is empty.
solution:
def non_start(a, b):
    return a[1:] + b[1:]
hints: Slicing from index 1 to the end drops just the first character.
This slice works fine even on empty strings — it just returns empty.
explainer: a[1:] and b[1:] each skip past index 0, removing the first character, and adding the two results together joins what remains.

title: Left2
brief: Moves the first two characters of a string to the end.
description: Take the first two characters off the front of the string and move them to the back instead. If the string has fewer than 2 characters, just return it unchanged.
hints: Check the length first — anything shorter than 2 characters stays the same.
Otherwise, swap the order of the two slices: everything after index 2, then the first two characters.
explainer: Once we know the string is long enough, s[2:] gives everything past the first two letters, and putting s[:2] after it swaps their order.

title: Right2
concept: Rearranging string slices from the end
brief: Moves the last two characters of a string to the front.
description: Take the last two characters off the end of the string and move them to the front instead. If the string has fewer than 2 characters, just return it unchanged.
hints: Check the length first — anything shorter than 2 characters stays the same.
Otherwise, grab the last two characters with s[-2:] and put them ahead of s[:-2].
explainer: s[-2:] pulls out the last two letters, and putting that in front of s[:-2] (everything except those last two letters) rearranges the string as asked.

title: The End
brief: Returns the last character of a string, or an empty string if it has none.
description: Return just the very last character of the given string. If the string is empty, there is no last character, so return an empty string instead.
hints: Check for the empty string case before indexing, or it will crash.
s[-1] gives you the final character of a non-empty string.
explainer: Testing for the empty string first avoids an index error, and s[-1] otherwise always reaches the last character no matter how long the string is.

title: Has Bad
brief: Checks whether the word 'bad' appears anywhere in the string.
description: Look through the given string and return true if the exact letters 'bad' show up anywhere inside it, in a row. Otherwise return false.
solution:
def has_bad(s):
    return "bad" in s
hints: The 'in' keyword checks if one string is tucked inside another.
The three letters need to be right next to each other in that exact order.
explainer: The in operator scans the whole string looking for that exact sequence of characters, so it finds "bad" wherever it's hiding.

title: At First
brief: Returns the first two characters of a string, padding with 'x' if it's too short.
description: Return the first two characters of the given string. If the string is too short to have two characters, pad it out with the letter 'x' until it does.
hints: Handle the three length cases separately: 2+ characters, exactly 1, and 0.
A single character just needs one 'x' added after it to reach length 2.
explainer: When the string already has 2 or more characters we just slice normally; otherwise we add enough 'x' characters to reach a length of exactly 2.

title: Last Chars
concept: Combining the last characters of two strings
brief: Builds a two-letter string from the last character of each input string.
description: Given two strings, take the last character of the first one and the last character of the second one, then join them together. If either string is empty, treat its last character as an empty piece.
solution:
def last_chars(a, b):
    last_a = a[-1] if a else ""
    last_b = b[-1] if b else ""
    return last_a + last_b
hints: Guard each string with a check for emptiness before grabbing s[-1].
Once you have both last characters (or empty pieces), just add them together.
explainer: Checking `if a` before indexing avoids crashing on an empty string, so each side safely contributes either its last letter or nothing at all.

title: ConCat
brief: Joins two strings together, one right after the other.
description: Given two strings, stick them together in the order they were given, with nothing extra added in between.
solution:
def con_cat(a, b):
    return a + b
hints: The + operator between two strings just lines them up back to back.
No spaces or extra characters are added — just a and b next to each other.
explainer: The + operator on strings concatenates them directly, so a + b always produces a followed immediately by b.

title: Lone Teen
brief: Checks whether exactly one of two numbers is a teen number (13 through 19).
description: A teen number is any whole number from 13 to 19. Given two numbers, return true only if exactly one of them is a teen number — if both are teens, or neither is, return false.
solution:
def lone_teen(a, b):
    a_teen = 13 <= a <= 19
    b_teen = 13 <= b <= 19
    return a_teen != b_teen
hints: Figure out separately whether each number is a teen, using 13 <= n <= 19.
'Exactly one is true' is the same as saying the two boolean results are different.
explainer: Comparing the two boolean teen checks with != gives True exactly when one is a teen and the other isn't, which is the 'lone' condition we want.

title: Del Del
concept: Scanning a string and skipping matched pieces
brief: Removes every 'del' found in a string, unless it's part of the word pattern 'dell'.
description: Scan through the string and remove every occurrence of the letters 'del'. As a special case, if a 'del' is immediately followed by another letter 'l' (making it look like the start of 'dell'), leave that one alone instead of removing it.
hints: Walk through the string one position at a time with an index, rather than character by character with a for loop.
At each position, peek ahead 3 characters to check for 'del', and one more to check the protection rule.
explainer: The loop looks 3 characters ahead at every position; when it finds 'del' not immediately followed by another 'l', it skips those 3 characters entirely instead of copying them into the result.

title: Front Again
concept: Comparing the first and last characters
brief: Checks whether a string's first character shows up again as its last character.
description: Return true if the first character of the string is the same as the last character. An empty string has no characters to compare, so it should return false.
solution:
def front_again(s):
    return len(s) > 0 and s[0] == s[-1]
hints: Check for the empty string first, since it has no first or last character.
s[0] and s[-1] grab the front and back characters for comparison.
explainer: Guarding with len(s) > 0 keeps us from indexing an empty string, and then comparing s[0] to s[-1] checks whether the front letter repeats at the end.

title: Make Out
brief: Checks whether the word 'out' shows up anywhere in the string.
description: Look through the given string and return true if the letters 'out' appear anywhere inside it, one right after another. Otherwise return false.
solution:
def make_out(s):
    return "out" in s
hints: The 'in' keyword checks whether one string sits inside another.
It doesn't matter where 'out' shows up — front, middle, or end all count.
explainer: The in operator searches the whole string for that exact sequence of letters, so it returns True as soon as 'out' appears anywhere at all.
